title: Automating Daily LinkedIn Drafts from GitHub
angle: Built a GitHub Action that selects a repo, uses Groq LLM for copy, renders code-snippet images, and sends drafts via Telegram.
post:
I was spending 15 minutes every morning copying code snippets into LinkedIn drafts - until I let a GitHub Action handle it.

The repo github-to-linkedin-poster runs daily at 08:00 UAE, picks one of my repositories, asks Groq to write a post, renders a highlighted code image, and pushes the draft to Telegram.

-> The workflow pulls raw LLM output and isolates the `POST:` section, trimming whitespace and limiting length to stay within LinkedIn’s character cap.
-> It extracts the `FILE:` and `LINES:` markers, then reads the source file from the repo’s file map.
-> To keep images readable, the snippet is capped at 20 lines and excess indentation is stripped before highlighting.
-> The final HTML/CSS is sent to hcti.io, which returns a PNG that the Telegram bot delivers.

Balancing automation with readability meant adding safety checks - like ignoring empty snippets and enforcing a minimum line count - so every draft looks polished without manual tweaks.

How do you handle content length limits when generating posts from code automatically?

title: Comparing XGBoost vs Pretrained Models for LOLBin Detection
angle: Explains the technical challenge of selecting and benchmarking machine-learning models to balance detection accuracy and interpretability.
post:
Balancing detection accuracy with model interpretability for LOLBin abuse meant I had to compare a classic tree-based classifier against a large pretrained language model.

SentinelLOLBins explores whether a lightweight XGBoost model can match the detection power of SecureBERT while still offering clear feature importance for analysts.

Here is the core of it:
-> I chose XGBClassifier with 300 trees, max depth 6 and a 0.8 subsample rate to keep the model expressive yet tractable.
-> The same hyper-parameters are fixed across runs to isolate the effect of data splits rather than tuning noise.
-> I train on the curated “train” set and validate on a separate “val” split, feeding the validation data to XGBoost’s early-stop-like eval_set mechanism.
-> After fitting, I evaluate precision, recall and F1 on a held-out test set, then sweep thresholds on the validation probabilities to select a decision point that favors low false-positives.

The exercise reminded me that a well-engineered baseline can provide comparable security coverage while preserving the transparency needed for incident response.

What strategies do you use to keep ML models both performant and explainable in security tooling?

title: Generating Watch Sketches with SVG from Measurements
angle: Explain how product dimensions are turned into scalable SVG illustrations without photos, highlighting the algorithm and rendering pipeline.
post:
Turning millimetre-level case specs into vector watch sketches eliminated any reliance on product photos. Chronos & Steel is a Next.js storefront that displays each watch as an SVG generated directly from its measurements. The goal was to keep the visual catalogue lightweight while staying true to the engineering data. Here is the core of it: ```tsx {PRODUCTS.map((product) => { const variants = buildVariants(product); const shown = variants.slice(0, 4); return (

{product.model} · {product.caseSpec.diameterMm}mm / {product.caseSpec.bezel} / {variants.length} variants

{(["card", "full"] as const).map((detail) => ( ``` -> Store dimensions (diameter, bezel, dial, strap) in the product record. -> `buildVariants` enumerates every legal combination, then `` receives the selected specs and builds SVG paths on the fly. -> The page uses `dynamic = "force-static"` so the SVGs are pre-rendered at build time, delivering instant load and perfect scalability. -> Skipping raster images keeps the bundle small and the illustrations crisp at any zoom level. Generating graphics from source data keeps the visual layer in lockstep with the database and removes an entire photo-handling pipeline.
